comparator.academicYear: 2025-2026 (current formally adopted Education and Examination Regulations for FASoS Bachelor's programmes in Arts and Culture, Digital Society and European Studies; independently corroborated by the current official programme pages checked 2026-09-27 for the Fall-2026 entrant cohort, since no distinct 2026-2027 edition of this EER bundle was found)
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from Maastricht University's current official Arts and Culture programme pages (overview, 'Courses & curriculum', 'Why this programme' and 'Your future', all checked 2026-09-27) and the current formally adopted 'Education and Examination Regulations Bachelor's programmes in Arts and Culture, Digital Society and European Studies 2025-2026' (s4, FASoS EER), which took effect 1 September 2025 and whose Section 2 (Admission) already applies to the 2026/27 admissions cohort; no distinct 2026-2027 edition of this FASoS bachelor EER bundle was found via reasonable search at time of check (a separate 2026-2027 EER exists for the unrelated Global Studies bachelor and for FASoS Master's programmes, confirming FASoS does republish yearly EERs when curriculum changes, so its absence here indicates no material change for Arts and Culture rather than an oversight), so the 2025-2026 EER is used as the controlling formally adopted source per Section 2.1, independently corroborated by the current official programme pages, which describe the identical three-phase structure, name the identical five semester-4/5 elective questions, and confirm a September start consistent with the fixed Fall-2026 UCR cohort. Article 3.1.1 describes the programme as an interdisciplinary study of Western society's challenges through the intersection of art, science/technology, media and politics, combining history, philosophy, art/literature studies and the qualitative social sciences (conceptual analysis, discourse analysis, ethnography, historical document analysis); this is independently corroborated by the current 'Why this programme' and overview pages verbatim. The registry's normalized target cp-000121 (row 122, source_provider_id 113A920, recognized_programme_code 50004, programme_unit_code 1001O5622, languages_json=["ENG"]) is the generic English-taught Bachelor Arts and Culture; the EER contains no afstudeerrichting, track or specialization for this programme (no occurrence of 'afstudeerrichting', 'track', 'specialisation' or 'specialization' anywhere in the EER's Arts and Culture sections), so routeSelection is null. Article 3.5 fixes the total study load at 180 credits (one credit = 28 hours); Article 3.6.1 sets out the complete compulsory structure across two phases. The Elementary phase (Year 1 and the first semester of Year 2; semesters 1-3) comprises 96 credits: Year 1 (60 credits) is Research and Writing I (7, English strand per Article 3.3.1 since the registry target's language is English; the Dutch-medium alternative ACU1901 is not selected), Mentor Programme 1 (1), Apollo and Dionysus (9) with Academic Reading Across Disciplines (4), Knowledge and Criticism (9) with Finding Sources (4), Disenchantment and Ideology (9) with Doing Conceptual Analysis (4), and Art and Modernity (9) with Analysing Arts (4); Year 2's first semester (36 credits) is Research and Writing II (9, English strand), the non-compulsory zero-credit Mentor Programme (not separately encoded as a component, consistent with the treatment of equivalent zero-credit mentoring components in other FASoS programmes), Technological Society (9) with Doing Ethnography (5), and Cultural Pluralism (9) with Doing Discourse Analysis (4). The Graduation phase (remainder of Year 2 and Year 3; semesters 4-6) comprises 84 credits. Semester 4 offers a restricted choice of one of three 9-credit courses (Othering Europe / Art, Literature and Technoscience / Living in a Digital Age) and, paired with it, a restricted choice of one of three skills (Research Methods: Advanced Document Analysis, 4 credits; Research Methods: Interviewing, 4 credits; or Analysing Arts II, 3 credits); semester 5 offers a parallel restricted choice of one of three further 9-credit courses (Power and Democracy / Vulnerable Bodies / Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change) paired with a restricted choice of one of two 3-credit skills (Doing Conceptual Analysis II / Doing Discourse Analysis II). The EER's own footnote states that choosing either 4-credit semester-4 skill raises the graduation phase from 84 to 85 credits, which arithmetically confirms that the EER's own baseline 84-credit reconstruction assumes the 3-credit Analysing Arts II option (9+3+9+3=24 credits for semester 4 and 5 together, plus the 14-credit semester-6 load below, totals exactly the stated 38 credits for 'semester 4 and 6' combined); Analysing Arts II is therefore selected as the only internally consistent choice for that specific restricted skill slot, independent of any programme-interest evidence. For the two 9-credit restricted course choices and the semester-5 skill choice, no formal EC consequence distinguishes the options, so the current official curriculum's own listing order is used as the neutral tie-break per Section 2.1 (first-listed option in each restricted choice: Othering Europe; Power and Democracy; Doing Conceptual Analysis II); both selected 9-credit courses are additionally and independently corroborated as the programme's own most prominent semester-4/5 themes by the current official 'Courses & curriculum' page, which names 'marginalised groups... represented in history, public debate and literature' and 'what does and could it mean to be a democratic society today' among its five headline semester-4/5 questions, matching Othering Europe and Power and Democracy exactly, and matching two of this exact target's own five generator-eligible Stable study direction programme-interest rows ('marginalised voices and cultural representation'; 'democracy, citizenship and public culture'). Semester 5 additionally comprises 30 credits of genuinely free elective units of study (a minor, study abroad, internship, faculty electives, or electives at another institution); no target-specific evidence favours one instantiation, so, consistent with Section 2.1, this space is preserved generically as a single open-elective component rather than invented. Semester 6 (Article 3.6.1) comprises Doing Research in Arts and Culture (7, compulsory) with a restricted choice of the English or Dutch Writing a Research Proposal (7; English strand selected per Article 3.3.1, since students who complete Research and Writing I/II in English must also write their research proposal and thesis in English) and the 16-credit Bachelor Thesis (English strand, ACU3905). Article 1.2's definition of 'praktische oefening' names writing a thesis and conducting a research assignment as its own worked examples; among the compulsory units, the 16-credit Bachelor Thesis is the programme's one identifiable independent-research capstone, so it is recorded as researchComponentId; Doing Research in Arts and Culture and Writing a Research Proposal are the immediately preceding methods/proposal-design training for that thesis rather than the thesis itself. 96 (Elementary) + 24 (semester 4) + 30 (semester 5 electives) + 30 (semester 6: 7+7+16) = 180 EC exactly. Article 3.1.1's final qualifications (Dublin Descriptors I-V) independently corroborate this reconstruction, naming interdisciplinary analysis of art/science/technology/media/politics as cultural phenomena, historical and philosophical grounding, humanities-and-qualitative-social-science methods (conceptual analysis, discourse analysis, ethnography, document analysis), academic writing/argumentation and supervised interdisciplinary research as the programme's own defining learning outcomes -- independently corroborated by the current official 'Your future' page naming policy advisor, media/editorial roles, cultural entrepreneurship/curation and further academic research as its named graduate outcomes. No further official source needed to be consulted: the current official overview/curriculum/why-this-programme/your-future pages and the current formally adopted EER together establish a complete, internally consistent, entirely accounted-for 180-EC pathway with explicit EC for every compulsory unit, an explicit arithmetic basis for the one forced restricted-skill selection, an explicit official-order tie-break for the two unforced restricted course selections (independently corroborated by target-specific programme-interest evidence), and an explicit, UCR-independent judgment (preserving rather than instantiating the 30-EC semester-5 elective space) fixed before any UCR course was considered. The distinct curriculum.maastrichtuniversity.nl mirror listed in the registry's registry_urls_json was attempted but was unreachable to available tools (DNS/network resolution failure via the configured egress proxy); the www.maastrichtuniversity.nl programme pages used above provide the same current content and are the pages a prospective Fall-2026 applicant is actually directed to from the programme's official overview page.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Interdisciplinary study of contemporary societal challenges through the intersecting cultural domains of art, science/technology, media and politics
Historical development of Western culture and thought from antiquity to the twenty-first century, tracing the deep historical roots of present-day societal problems
Philosophical, ethical and conceptual analysis of the ideas, norms and values shaping Western culture, and the social and ethical implications of cultural change
Critical, interdisciplinary humanities-and-qualitative-social-science analysis of cultural texts, artefacts, practices, discourses and institutions
Qualitative research methods -- ethnography, discourse analysis, (historical) document analysis and conceptual analysis -- applied to cultural phenomena
Literary and artistic analysis of texts, artworks and cultural representations
Academic writing, structured argumentation and public debate about contemporary cultural and social questions
Independent scholarly research on a self-chosen arts-and-culture topic, culminating in the Bachelor thesis
adjacent: Marginalised voices and cultural representation: how the voices and experiences of marginalised groups are represented or excluded in history, public debate and literature
Technology, ethics and the arts: the ethical issues raised by emerging technologies and how art and literature help explore them
Democracy, citizenship and public culture: what it does and could mean to be a democratic society today
Culture and climate change: how scientists, states, activists and industry understand and respond to climate change on a global scale
Bodies, identity and social norms: how social norms about the body are constructed, challenged or transformed
questions: Illustrative or temporary applied formats used to communicate cultural research and analysis (producing a podcast, curating an arts festival, writing a cultural-policy brief)

Graduate career and further-study trajectories the programme prepares students for (cultural policy and arts administration, museum and heritage careers, journalism/media/communication careers, education and cultural research)

alternatives.label: Interdisciplinary Cultural Studies: History, Philosophy, Literature and the Arts
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by history (4 of 24: Modern History, Western Way of War, History Research Seminar, Native American Histories), philosophy (3: Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind), literature (3: Introduction to Literary Studies, Life & Travel Writing, Film & Text) and art/cultural heritage (4: Introduction to World Archaeology, Introduction to Western Art History, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Greek Archaeology), reinforced by a communication/rhetoric cluster (3: Rhetoric in Action, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Creative Communication Laboratory) and a qualitative-methods/social-theory cluster (2: Qualitative Research Methodology, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory), with a light politics/law/media thread (Introduction to Political Philosophy, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Public International Law, Introduction to Film & Media) completing the interdisciplinary combination the comparator's own doelstelling (Article 3.1.1) names as defining the field. The label names history, philosophy, literature and the arts as the four disciplinary anchors that together account for 14 of the 24 scheduled courses and reproduce the comparator's own combination of humanities disciplines and qualitative social science.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to Maastricht's generalist Bachelor Arts and Culture (the EER confirms no formal afstudeerrichting exists for this normalized target): a shared interdisciplinary humanities core -- the history of Western culture and political ideology, philosophical and ethical analysis of ideas and norms, literary and artistic analysis of texts and artworks, and critical social theory -- combined with UCR's own academic-writing/rhetoric sequence and qualitative research methods training to reproduce the programme's own combination of history, philosophy, art/literature studies and the qualitative social sciences studying art, science/technology, media and politics as cultural phenomena, while leaving the 30-EC semester-5 elective space honestly preserved as unclaimed elective space and several specialist components (ethnography, discourse analysis and conceptual-analysis skills training as dedicated modules, and the programme's own semester-4/5 thematic specialisations) genuinely unmatched.
progression: GOSGATE102 (semester 1, no formal prerequisite) precedes Introduction to Public International Law (semester 4), which formally requires it. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 1, within Year 1. Introductory gateway and level-1 courses (Modern History, Introduction to Western Philosophy, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to World Archaeology, Introduction to Literary Studies, Introduction to Western Art History, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Introduction to Film & Media, Introduction to Political Philosophy) are concentrated in semesters 1-3, and level-3 advanced work (History Research Seminar, Film & Text, Modern Art & Modern Museums, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory, Native American Histories, Creative Communication Laboratory) is concentrated in semesters 4-6, so that foundational orientation precedes advanced work where a reasonable sequence is available. Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.

alternatives.label: Technology, Ethics and the Arts in a Digital Age
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum retains a shared humanities anchor (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Western Art History, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Introduction to Literary Studies, Film & Text, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Rhetoric in Action, Persuasive Communication, Law Society & Justice) but replaces the closest match's history/heritage/politics breadth with UCR's full available artificial-intelligence, data-science and digital-media offerings (AI Ethics, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Database Management Systems, Mathematical Methods, Business & Economy in the Age of AI, Media Archaeology, From T.V. to TikTok, The Documentary) together with a deepened philosophy-of-mind/ethics cluster (Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Free Will Time & the Self) -- 11 of 24 courses concentrated on technology, AI and digital media. The label names technology and ethics first for the dominant AI/data-science-plus-normative-philosophy cluster and the arts second for the media/literature/art-history courses that examine how art and digital culture represent and respond to these technologies.
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different second UCR route evidenced by the target's own Stable study direction programme-interest row 'technology, ethics and art', independently corroborated by the current official curriculum page's own semester-4 elective question 'what ethical issues do emerging technologies raise, and how can art help explore them?' and by the semester-4 course Art, Literature and Technoscience / Living in a Digital Age: a concentration retaining the shared philosophy, literature, art-history and rhetoric core but replacing the closest match's history/heritage/politics breadth with UCR's full available artificial-intelligence, data-science, media-history and philosophy-of-mind offerings, examining how digital technology and artificial intelligence transform culture, art, media and ethical life.
progression: DISGATE102 (semester 2, no formal prerequisite) precedes Neural Networks & Deep Learning (semester 6), which formally requires it. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 2, within Year 1. Introductory gateway and level-1 courses (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Western Art History, AI Ethics [available from semester 2], Introduction to Data Science, Database Management Systems, Media Archaeology, Introduction to Literary Studies, The Art of Rhetorical Communication) are concentrated in semesters 1-3, and level-3 advanced work (Film & Text, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Persuasive Communication, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, The Documentary) is concentrated in semesters 5-6, so that foundational orientation precedes advanced work where a reasonable sequence is available. Free Will, Time & the Self is a level-300 course scheduled in semester 1: it carries no formal prerequisite, its philosophical content on personal identity and agency does not presuppose completion of any other scheduled course, and UCR's open curriculum permits this early placement (a 300-level designation does not by itself prohibit it). Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.

examines theories of mind, consciousness and cognition, directly implementing the technology-ethics-and-the-arts adjacent direction's engagement with questions of mind raised by artificial intelligence
alternatives.distinctness: Maastricht's Bachelor Arts and Culture names 'technology, ethics and art' as one of its own five generator-eligible Stable study direction programme-interest rows and offers a corresponding semester-4 elective (Art, Literature and Technoscience / Living in a Digital Age) addressing exactly this combination, independently corroborated by the current official curriculum page's own semester-4 framing question about the ethics of emerging technologies. The closest match already includes a light politics/law thread but no artificial-intelligence or data-science content at all. This alternative goes materially further: it retains the identical philosophy/literature/art-history/rhetoric core (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Western Art History, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Introduction to Literary Studies, Film & Text, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Rhetoric in Action, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Film & Media, Personal & Professional Development -- 10 of 24 courses shared with the closest match) but replaces 12 of the closest match's remaining courses (Modern History, Western Way of War, History Research Seminar, Native American Histories, Introduction to World Archaeology, Greek Archaeology, Qualitative Research Methodology, New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory, Life & Travel Writing, Introduction to Public International Law, Creative Communication Laboratory, Introduction to Political Philosophy) with UCR's AI Ethics, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Database Management Systems, Mathematical Methods, Business & Economy in the Age of AI, Media Archaeology, From T.V. to TikTok, The Documentary, Philosophy of Mind and Free Will Time & the Self, for a total of twelve technology/AI/media/philosophy-of-mind courses concentrating the programme on the ethical and cultural consequences of contemporary technology. This is a material curricular consequence, not cosmetic reshuffling: it changes the alternative's academic priorities from a generalist history-and-heritage-led humanities programme to a single-domain technology-and-ethics concentration, and the two alternatives share 12 of 24 courses while differing in 12 of 24 each way (90 EC), comfortably exceeding the pairwise 30-EC/4-course minimum.

alternatives.label: Culture, Media and the Politics of Environmental Change
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum retains a shared humanities/social-science anchor (Modern History, Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Western Art History, Introduction to Literary Studies, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Film & Media, Qualitative Research Methodology, Personal & Professional Development) but replaces the closest match's history/heritage/literature breadth with UCR's full available sustainability, environmental-science and governance offerings (Sustainability Essentials I & II, Climate Change, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Living with Water, Governance of Sustainability, Environmental Biogeochemistry) together with a politics/law cluster addressing international governance (European Union Politics, Foundations of European Union Law, Peace & Conflict, Introduction to Public International Law) and media/communication courses addressing environmental representation (Media & the Environment, Communicating the Climate Crisis, Social Movements & Environmental Justice) -- 11 of 24 courses concentrated on climate, sustainability and environmental governance. The label names culture and media first for the retained humanities and communication anchor, and the politics of environmental change second for the sustainability/governance cluster that organises this alternative's distinctive academic priorities.
alternatives.concept: A genuinely different third UCR route evidenced by the target's own Stable study direction programme-interest row 'culture and climate change', independently corroborated by the current official curriculum page's own semester-5 elective question 'how do scientists, states, activists and industry understand and respond to climate change on a global scale?' and by the semester-5 course Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change: a concentration retaining the shared history, philosophy, art-history, rhetoric and qualitative-methods core but replacing the closest match's literary and heritage-specialist depth with UCR's full available sustainability, environmental-science, governance and environmental-media offerings, studying how culture, media, science and political authority together shape responses to climate and environmental change.
progression: Sustainability Essentials I (semester 1, no formal prerequisite) precedes Sustainability Essentials II (semester 2) and Environmental Biogeochemistry (semester 5), both of which formally require it. Law Society & Justice (semester 1, no formal prerequisite) precedes Introduction to Public International Law (semester 4) and Foundations of European Union Law (semester 6), both of which formally require it. Personal & Professional Development is scheduled in semester 2, within Year 1. Introductory gateway and level-1 courses (Sustainability Essentials I, Law Society & Justice, Modern History, Introduction to Western Philosophy, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Climate Change, Introduction to Film & Media, Introduction to Western Art History) are concentrated in semesters 1-3, and level-3 advanced work (Governance of Sustainability, Foundations of European Union Law, European Union Politics, Peace & Conflict, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Environmental Biogeochemistry) is concentrated in semesters 4-6, so that foundational orientation precedes advanced work where a reasonable sequence is available. Every course is offered in its assigned semester under the fixed Fall 2026 cohort schedule.
alternatives.distinctness: Maastricht's Bachelor Arts and Culture names 'culture and climate change' as one of its own five generator-eligible Stable study direction programme-interest rows and offers a corresponding semester-5 elective (Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change) addressing exactly this theme, independently corroborated by the current official curriculum page's own semester-5 framing question about global responses to climate change. Neither the closest match nor the technology-and-ethics alternative includes any sustainability, environmental-science or environmental-governance content. This alternative goes materially further than either: measured against the closest match, it retains 10 of 24 courses (Modern History, Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Western Art History, Introduction to Literary Studies, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Public International Law, Introduction to Film & Media, Qualitative Research Methodology, Personal & Professional Development) and replaces the remaining 14 (Western Way of War, History Research Seminar, Native American Histories, Introduction to World Archaeology, Greek Archaeology, Modern Art & Modern Museums, Life & Travel Writing, Film & Text, Rhetoric in Action, Creative Communication Laboratory, Introduction to Political Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Introduction to Political Philosophy's political-philosophy framing) with UCR's Sustainability Essentials I & II, Climate Change, Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy, Research in a Sustainable Delta, Living with Water, Governance of Sustainability, Environmental Biogeochemistry, Social Movements & Environmental Justice, Media & the Environment, Communicating the Climate Crisis, European Union Politics, Foundations of European Union Law and Peace & Conflict, for a total of fourteen sustainability/environmental-governance/environmental-media courses, differing in 14 of 24 courses each way (105 EC). Measured against the technology-and-ethics alternative, the two share only 7 of 24 courses (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Introduction to Western Art History, Introduction to Literary Studies, The Art of Rhetorical Communication, Law Society & Justice, Introduction to Film & Media, Personal & Professional Development) and differ in 17 of 24 courses each way (127.5 EC). Both pairwise differences comfortably exceed the 30-EC/4-course minimum. This is a material curricular consequence, not cosmetic reshuffling: it changes the alternative's academic priorities from a generalist or technology-led humanities programme to a single-domain environmental-culture-and-governance concentration.

selection.assessment: The closest match directly owns fourteen generator-eligible rows: understanding contemporary culture and society; how art, science, media and politics shape one another; the historical roots of present-day problems; the social and ethical implications of cultural change; critical cultural analysis; interdisciplinary humanities and social-science perspectives; conceptual and philosophical analysis; historical document research; ethnographic research; literary and artistic analysis; discourse analysis; academic writing and argumentation; debating cultural and social questions; and independent research in arts and culture -- all of which describe the programme's own general interdisciplinary core, methods pluralism and academic-skills orientation rather than an independent substantive direction, and are therefore substantively covered by the closest match's own core concept rather than forced into a residual candidate. The remaining five generator-eligible rows are the target's own five Stable study direction rows, each corresponding one-to-one with one of the programme's own current official semester-4/5 elective specialisations (independently confirmed by the official 'Courses & curriculum' page's own five framing questions): 'marginalised voices and cultural representation' (Othering Europe); 'technology, ethics and art' (Art, Literature and Technoscience / Living in a Digital Age); 'democracy, citizenship and public culture' (Power and Democracy); 'culture and climate change' (Authority, Expertise and Environmental Change); and 'bodies, identity and social norms' (Vulnerable Bodies). Each of the five is independently assessed as its own coherent candidate direction: none is an omnibus residual, and each is evidence-backed by the programme's own official curriculum structure as well as by the target-specific programme-interest row. Two were selected for development into Alternative 2 and Alternative 3: 'technology, ethics and art' and 'culture and climate change'. Both pass all four gates -- each is evidence-backed by a generator-eligible row independently corroborated by the programme's own current official curriculum page; each has a clear organising logic; each is substantively distinct, drawing on UCR's DIS/BEN artificial-intelligence and data-science offerings, or its ENS sustainability and environmental-science offerings respectively, departments the closest match does not use at all, replacing 12 and 14 of the closest match's 24 courses respectively (90 EC and 105 EC) and differing from each other by 17 courses (127.5 EC); and each is mechanically feasible against the enriched course database, with six distinct level-300 courses and pairwise differences comfortably exceeding the 30-EC/4-course floor against both other included alternatives. These two were selected for development, rather than the remaining three, because their organising logic draws most heavily on UCR departments genuinely outside the closest match's own interdisciplinary-humanities core (data science/AI and environmental science respectively), producing the clearest and most materially distinct curricula; the remaining three candidates ('marginalised voices and cultural representation', 'democracy, citizenship and public culture', 'bodies, identity and social norms') would each be built substantially from the same GOS/MCC/HCB course pool the closest match already draws on, and are recorded as 'maximum-reached': each remains a coherent, evidence-backed candidate direction that was not developed into a fourth alternative because the production ceiling of three alternatives was already reached by the two candidates above. No generator-eligible evidence remains unassigned: the closest match's fourteen owned rows and the five candidates' fifteen generating rows together account for all nineteen generator-eligible interest items (fifty-seven individual registry rows) linked to this target. Production therefore includes the maximum of three alternatives and records 'maximum-reached' as the stopping state.

notes.text: All three UCR alternatives include substantial study of the comparator's shared interdisciplinary humanities core (history, philosophy, literature, art history and rhetoric). The comparator additionally trains ethnography, discourse analysis and conceptual analysis as separately credited 'Doing...' skills modules paired with specific content courses; UCR teaches related qualitative-methods content (through Qualitative Research Methodology and within its content courses) but does not offer these methods as discrete, separately credited skills modules of the same kind.

Maastricht pairs each Elementary-phase content course with its own separately credited 'Doing...' or 'Analysing...' skills module (e.g. Apollo and Dionysus with Academic Reading Across Disciplines, Art and Modernity with Analysing Arts) and structures its Graduation phase around named restricted-choice semester-4/5 electives addressing marginalised voices, technology/ethics, democracy, climate change and the body. At UCR, comparable methods training and thematic specialisation are distributed across separate whole courses rather than organised as paired content-plus-skill modules or as a single shared restricted-choice slot; the UCR alternatives therefore approach related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the comparator's own module format.
